stories.headline: A look inside the Somali mall where Omar reappeared after DC raid raises more failed assimilation concerns
stories.note: Ilhan Omar's troubles keep growing two days before the midterms.
body: A day after Rep. Ilhan Omar's first public appearance since federal agents raided her home, Fox News Digital toured the Minneapolis mall where she resurfaced: the Karmel Mall of Somalia.

The mall is owned by Basim Sabri, a Gaza-born real estate investor with ties across Minnesota politics who is friends with Omar and knew her father. Omar had lunch there with supporters and state Attorney General Keith Ellison after casting an early ballot in her own race.

Inside, English is mostly a second language. Shops sell overseas SIM cards, money exchange and travel to East Africa and the Middle East, and a giant Somali flag is painted on the food court ceiling. Fox's crew was initially stopped by security until Sabri approved filming. Sabri says the mall helps Somalis integrate and prosper, and he once banned Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey over a Gaza ceasefire veto.

The Center for Immigration Studies' Steven Camarota pointed to a report finding more than half of children in Somali-born households in Minnesota live in poverty, 89% of Somali households get some form of welfare, and half of long-term Somali immigrants can't speak English very well. He blamed modern technology, elite attitudes that treat assimilation as a dirty word, and record immigration levels.
Sabri himself served a federal prison sentence after a 2005 bribery conviction involving a Minneapolis official, a history he discussed with Fox.

Why it matters: With Omar under federal investigation days before the midterms, the story keeps her and questions about assimilation in her district front and center, an ongoing headache for Democrats.

stories.headline: 'Toxic cocktail' of renter protections destroyed $39M affordable housing investment as Dem cities follow suit
stories.note: Seattle's progressive housing rules backfired, costing a $39M affordable housing investment.
body: Seattle's pile of renter-protection rules allegedly sank a $39 million affordable housing investment, and the owners just won the right to take the city to court over it.

Washington's Court of Appeals ruled Monday that GRE Downtowner LLC, owner of the 254-unit Addison on Fourth, can pursue claims that Seattle's rental regulations amounted to an unconstitutional taking of private property. The building was a federal low-income tax credit project serving lower-income tenants.

According to court filings, the property made money from 2015 to 2018. Then the city limited background checks, let tenants add occupants without the landlord's consent, restricted evictions and required relocation payments after certain rent hikes. GRE says rent collection fell from 93.9% in 2018 to 44.1% in 2023, with about $5.8 million in losses, and a federal judge put the property in receivership in January 2026.

Sean Flynn of the Rental Housing Association of Washington called it a "toxic cocktail of legislation" and said the cranes that once dotted Seattle's skyline are gone. GMU law professor Ilya Somin called the ruling moderately significant and said the roommate rule looks especially vulnerable. Seattle's city attorney's office said it hasn't decided whether to appeal.

Why it matters: Similar landlord rules exist in New York, San Francisco, Portland and Philadelphia. The case is a concrete example of progressive housing policy hurting the very low-income renters it was meant to protect.

stories.headline: Trump prosecutions under Biden set precedent for DOJ's Alaska 'Decoy Dan' probe, ex-FEC chair says
stories.note: A former FEC chair says Biden-era precedent leaves Democrats exposed in the Alaska Decoy Dan probe.
body: The Justice Department is investigating claims that Democratic operatives recruited Daniel J. Sullivan, nicknamed "Decoy Dan," to pull votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, and left-leaning election lawyers are calling it federal overreach.

Former FEC commissioner Hans von Spakovsky says Democrats set the precedent themselves. He points to Jack Smith's 2023 indictment of Trump, which relied on conspiracy to defraud the United States and conspiracy against rights, and says prosecutors could apply similar theories if operatives knowingly recruited a look-alike candidate to confuse voters.

Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman announced the probe Friday alongside the FBI and state troopers. DOJ amended its lawsuit to cite New York Times reporting that the DSCC and senior Peltola campaign aides worked to recruit spoiler candidates. Sources told Fox that more than 30 subpoenas went out in 24 hours, though Heyman wouldn't say what charges might come.

Critics including Common Cause and the progressive 907 Initiative say DOJ has no role in state election law and is trying to tip the race. Von Spakovsky called the scheme a "dirty trick" and said recruitment alone may not be a crime, but paying for or running the candidate's campaign could create campaign-finance violations.
Why it matters: Democrats spent years backing the legal theories used against Trump. Now those same theories could be turned on their own operatives in one of the Senate's most important races.

stories.headline: How House Democrats' 'deterrence message' on Trump jobs could backfire
stories.note: A former federal prosecutor warns House Democrats' threats toward Trump officials could backfire.
body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin's warning to young Americans not to take Trump administration jobs could hand Trump officials a legal weapon against future Democratic investigations, a former Trump DOJ official says.
At an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event, the Michigan Democrat said she wants her party to bring "signature cases" against officials who helped Trump, adding, "I want that deterrence message sent."

Abhishek Kambli, a former deputy associate attorney general now at Holtzman Vogel, says the Supreme Court's Trump v. Mazars test requires a real legislative purpose for subpoenas, and remarks like Slotkin's give anyone challenging them a record showing the goal is punishment. He also warned that "the process is the punishment" for young staffers who can't afford lawyers.

Florida State law professor Michael Morley was more skeptical that courts would toss subpoenas over partisan comments, but he called it "bad atmospherics" that could make judges marginally less sympathetic. Slotkin told CNN she meant only officials who break the law and called the criticism manufactured outrage.
Why it matters: As Democrats plan probes of the Trump family and administration if they win Congress, their own campaign rhetoric could undercut those investigations in court.

stories.headline: Why the Ilhan Omar saga isn't going away
stories.note: The Omar saga stays a drag on Democrats heading into Election Day.
body: Rep. Ilhan Omar has become a staple of President Trump's rally speeches as DHS and DOJ probe her over alleged immigration fraud and financial disclosures, and Fox's Chad Pergram explains why the issue will follow Democrats past Election Day.

The New York Times reported that the Obama-era Justice Department looked into Omar in 2016 and found evidence of a possible fraudulent marriage. That inquiry ran into the Biden years before closing in 2021. If she was naturalized improperly, it could raise questions about whether she can serve in Congress at all.

Omar's spokeswoman calls it a "baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory," and former President Obama said the administration is targeting her for her views. Her GOP opponent John Nagel calls the accusations very serious, while Rep. Mike Lawler says the Ethics Committee should open an investigation as soon as the House returns.

The Constitution lets the House judge its members' qualifications. A motion to exclude Omar could come on Jan. 3, right when the new speaker swears in members, meaning newly elected swing-district Democrats could face a tough first vote on whether to seat her.
Why it matters: If Democrats win the House, the Omar question could force moderates into a damaging vote and split them from progressives, giving Republicans an early wedge issue in the new Congress.

stories.headline: Major US children's hospital opens historic detransition clinic after $10M legal showdown
stories.note: A major children's hospital opening a detransition clinic is a win for critics of gender medicine for kids.
body: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced that the nation's first detransition clinic is now open at Texas Children's Hospital, a result of his $10 million settlement with the hospital.

The settlement resolved claims that the hospital improperly billed Texas Medicaid for gender-transition treatments. It also requires the hospital to set up and fully fund the clinic for five years at no cost to patients and publicize it on its website. The clinic treats patients through age 21, plus related OB-GYN care for older patients.

Paxton said the clinic will help "victims of the radical left's gender ideology." A hospital spokesperson said the clinic is operational and complying with the settlement, offering services from endocrinology to psychiatry, and is triaging prospective patients, though no clinical appointments have happened yet.
Paxton is the GOP nominee in Texas' Senate race, where a recent Fox News poll had him tied with Democrat James Talarico at 49%. Trump campaigned for him in Corpus Christi and Lubbock this week.
Why it matters: The clinic gives Paxton a concrete win on an issue where Republicans hold the popular position, right as he heads into a dead-even Senate race.
